cases.case_name: State v. Strauch
cases.holding: The Court held that both privately and publicly employed licensed social workers are mandatory child-abuse reporters under NMSA 1978, Section 32A-4-3(A), so an alleged abuser's statements in private counseling sessions are not protected by the psychotherapist-patient privilege.
cases.quote: both privately and publicly employed social workers are mandatory child abuse reporters, in light of the statutory history and the broadly inclusive terms of the Abuse and Neglect Act

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling New Mexico Supreme Court construction of the Section 32A-4-3(A) reporting duty and of who counts as a mandatory reporter.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that the reporting duty in Section 32A-4-3(A) runs to 'every person,' which is the statutory basis for third-party and voluntary reports in New Mexico.
relevance.INP-06: Because the duty attaches to every person with a reasonable suspicion, hotline and anonymous intake in New Mexico rests on the same statutory obligation the Court construes here.
relevance.INP-07: It holds that counseling and therapy disclosures fall inside the reporting duty and outside the psychotherapist-patient privilege, the core issue at a medical or behavioral-health disclosure.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Mafin M.
cases.holding: Applying the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, the Court held that a mother's procedural due process rights were not violated when the district court terminated her parental rights at a hearing she did not attend, and it reinstated the termination.
cases.quote: because the right to raise one's child is a fundamental right protected by the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, termination proceedings must be conducted in a constitutional manner

relevance.INP-05: The case began when the mother herself called police and asked the State to take custody, and the Court treats that voluntary request as the lawful entry point into the dependency system.
relevance.ACT-02: It describes the dispositional order and court-approved treatment plan as the mechanism by which the court directs services after adjudication.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Pamela R.D.G.
cases.holding: The Court held that neglect and abuse proceedings must afford parents constitutional due process, and that admitting a non-testifying four-year-old's hearsay statements after the children's court examined their reliability did not deny the parents due process.
cases.quote: neglect and abuse proceedings must also be conducted in a manner that affords the parents constitutional due process

relevance.DEC-02: It governs how a child's out-of-court disclosures gathered during investigation may be used, and what reliability inquiry the court must make before relying on them.
relevance.DEC-03: It sets the due-process floor for the evidence on which a founded finding of abuse may rest when the child does not testify.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Keon H. (In re Anhayla H.)
cases.holding: The Court held that substantial evidence supported the district court's finding that CYFD made reasonable efforts to assist an incarcerated father under Section 32A-4-28(B)(2), reversed the Court of Appeals, and affirmed the termination of his parental rights.
cases.quote: In this case, the Department's efforts, although imperfect, were reasonable.

relevance.DEC-06: It confirms that CYFD's front-end offer of a treatment plan and services, even if imperfect, can satisfy the statutory efforts requirement before court compulsion escalates.
relevance.ACT-01: It illustrates that a parent's refusal to engage voluntarily with offered services is weighed against the parent, not against the agency.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading New Mexico Supreme Court statement on what a court-ordered treatment plan and CYFD's assistance with it must look like.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification turns on the reasonable-efforts finding this opinion reviews, including how efforts are assessed for an incarcerated parent.
relevance.PMC-01: Reasonable efforts is the state-law expression of the Title IV-E requirement CFSR measures, and this case shows how New Mexico courts review it.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the benchmark New Mexico authority any cross-chain analysis of reasonable-efforts compliance must be measured against.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Marlene C. (In re Esther V.)
cases.holding: The Court held that in a contested adjudication governed by ICWA the district court must always make the 25 U.S.C. Section 1912(d) and (e) findings at the adjudicatory stage, and separately held that New Mexico's ex parte and custody hearings are Section 1922 emergency proceedings to which Section 1912 does not apply; it reversed the neglect adjudication and remanded.
cases.quote: in a contested adjudication to which ICWA applies, the district court must always make the findings of fact required under § 1912(d) and (e) of ICWA at the adjudication stage

relevance.INP-11: This is New Mexico's controlling decision on when ICWA's federal standards attach once a child is identified as an Indian child.
relevance.INP-12: The same opinion holds that New Mexico's ex parte and custody hearings are emergency proceedings under 25 U.S.C. Section 1922, which is what permits protective custody before the ICWA findings are made.
relevance.DEC-04: It squarely addresses the legal status of an emergency removal of an Indian child taken before any Section 1912 findings exist.
relevance.DEC-05: It fixes the adjudicatory hearing, not the dispositional hearing, as the stage at which the petition must be supported by the ICWA findings.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court's reading of Section 1912(e) controls whether a contested foster placement of an Indian child may continue, which drives kinship and tribal placement decisions.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to make the ICWA findings at adjudication is a federal-compliance failure that voids the adjudication, as it did here.
relevance.FAIL-05: ICWA's protections are the principal statutory guard in New Mexico against removal decisions that disregard a child's tribal identity.
relevance.PMC-06: Any audit of New Mexico ICWA compliance starts from this holding about which hearing must carry the federal findings.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Djamila B. (In re Mahdjid B.)
cases.holding: The Court held that kinship guardians are not necessary and indispensable parties to abuse and neglect proceedings but have a statutory right to a Kinship Guardianship Act revocation hearing before they may be involuntarily dismissed from those proceedings.
cases.quote: kinship guardianships must be revoked in accordance with the revocation procedures of the KGA and our Rules of Evidence before involuntarily dismissing a kinship guardian from abuse and neglect proceedings

relevance.INP-05: It addresses the situation where a relative has already taken legal responsibility for a child under the Kinship Guardianship Act before CYFD becomes involved.
relevance.DEC-05: It determines who must be joined and heard once CYFD files an abuse and neglect petition involving a child already under kinship guardianship.
relevance.ACT-01: A Kinship Guardianship Act guardianship is the principal voluntary, non-court-compelled arrangement New Mexico families use, and this case protects it.
relevance.ACT-04: This is the controlling New Mexico authority on the legal status of a kinship caregiver once CYFD opens a case.
relevance.OUT-03: It holds that a kinship guardianship cannot be displaced as a permanency option without the KGA revocation procedure being followed first.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of Grace H.
cases.holding: The Court held that where a parent is present and willing to participate before termination, abandonment must be pursued under Section 32A-4-28(B)(2), which requires CYFD assistance and treatment, rather than under Section 32A-4-28(B)(1); it reversed the termination and remanded.
cases.quote: we hold that where a parent is present and willing to participate prior to termination, termination by abandonment must follow from Subsection (B)(2)

relevance.ACT-02: It ties the abandonment ground to the statutory requirement that the parent first be assessed and offered treatment under a plan.
relevance.OUT-01: It preserves the reunification pathway for a willing parent by forbidding CYFD from routing around the assistance requirement.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling New Mexico Supreme Court construction of which abandonment subsection may support termination.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a direct example of the Supreme Court vacating a termination because CYFD used the wrong statutory ground.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Douglas B.
cases.holding: The Court held that a court must analyze a qualified expert witness's qualifications independently for each of ICWA's two required categories of testimony, and that the witness here was qualified as to tribal cultural standards but not as to serious emotional or physical damage, requiring a new adjudicatory hearing.
cases.quote: courts must independently analyze qualification in the two categories of required QEW testimony under ICWA and that the testimony can come from one or multiple experts

relevance.INP-11: This is New Mexico's most recent Supreme Court decision on the ICWA qualified-expert-witness requirement that conditions removal and foster placement of an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-05: Accepting an unqualified expert on serious damage to an Indian child is precisely the kind of ICWA shortfall that produces disparate removal outcomes for tribal families.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Calvin T.
cases.holding: The Court held that a children's court may join 'any other person' under Rule 10-121(B)(4) NMRA only where that person is a necessary party under the Rule 1-019(A)(1) standard, and remanded for the children's court to apply that standard to the youth's managed care organization.
cases.quote: the set of parties necessary to afford complete relief sought in such proceedings will include those parties necessary to serve the best interests of the child

relevance.INP-04: It shows the children's court exercising its own authority to pull additional entities into an abuse and neglect case to obtain services for the child.
relevance.DEC-05: It defines the outer boundary of who may be made a party once a neglect or abuse petition is pending.
relevance.ACT-06: The motion arose from an imminent discharge from acute psychiatric care with no treatment foster placement identified, which is the emergency medical and psychological care problem this node covers.
relevance.OUT-04: The youth had been in CYFD custody since 2015 with repeated hospitalizations and placement disruptions, the classic older-youth trajectory toward aging out.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Mercer-Smith
cases.holding: The Court held that the purpose for which the district court exercised its contempt power against CYFD was not remedial and therefore could not be sustained as civil contempt, and it reversed the contempt order and vacated the nearly four-million-dollar award in its entirety.
cases.quote: we reverse the contempt order and vacate the award in its entirety

relevance.INP-04: It arose from a judicial placement order directed at CYFD and shows how far a court may go in enforcing such an order.
relevance.ACT-03: The underlying dispute was CYFD's foster placement of the children with former group-home employees in violation of the court's placement order.
relevance.ACT-05: It marks the limits of a court's coercive power to police an order restricting who may have contact with or custody of children in state care.
relevance.OUT-04: The Court notes that the children aged out of the system while the litigation dragged on, which is the practical cost of protracted permanency litigation.
relevance.OUT-05: It vacated the entire ancillary proceeding, illustrating how appellate review can unwind years of post-dispositional litigation.
relevance.PMC-03: It shows the limits of judicial, as opposed to citizen-panel or administrative, oversight of agency placement decisions.

cases.case_name: Kennedy v. Dexter Consolidated Schools
cases.holding: The Court held that school officials who strip-searched students without individualized suspicion violated clearly established Fourth Amendment law and were not entitled to qualified immunity, and it reinstated the jury's verdict against officials the Court of Appeals had immunized.
cases.quote: We hold that in light of the Tenth Circuit's affirmation of Renfrow, the unlawfulness of conducting a strip-to-undergarments search without individualized suspicion was clearly established in 1992

relevance.INP-08: It is New Mexico's leading decision on the constitutional limits of school-official investigation of a student's body, the setting in which many educational disclosures are generated.
relevance.DEC-02: It sets the individualized-suspicion floor for any intrusive search of a child conducted as part of an investigation on school grounds.

cases.case_name: Pacheco v. Hudson
cases.holding: The Court held that an Inspection of Public Records Act enforcement action seeking a district court's records must be filed against the lawfully designated IPRA custodian and in the judicial district that maintains the records.
cases.quote: IPRA actions directed at a district court's records must be filed against the lawfully designated IPRA custodian and must be filed in the judicial district that maintains the records

relevance.FAIL-06: It establishes how a requester enforces disclosure in New Mexico and against whom, which is the first obstacle in any transparency failure claim.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the controlling procedural framework for an IPRA request and suit, New Mexico's state analogue to FOIA.

cases.case_name: Republican Party v. New Mexico Taxation & Revenue Department
cases.holding: The Court held that New Mexico recognizes only a limited constitutional executive privilege that may be invoked by the Governor alone, and declined to recognize a common-law deliberative process privilege that would shield cabinet agency records from disclosure.
cases.quote: while the privilege can extend to communications authored by close advisers, the privilege's constitutional foundation requires limiting its invocation to the Governor

relevance.FAIL-06: It forecloses the broad deliberative-process objection agencies most often raise to withhold internal child-welfare records.
relevance.PMC-05: It defines the narrow universe of executive-privilege exceptions to New Mexico's public-records regime.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights of Eventyr J.
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that clear and convincing evidence supported the findings and that admitting the Citizen's Review Board chairman's testimony about the mother's statements to the Board did not deprive her of due process.
cases.quote: we conclude that there was clear and convincing evidence to support the district court's order terminating Respondent's parental rights and that Respondent's due process rights were not violated

relevance.INP-09: It is the New Mexico decision describing how the substitute care review board process under Section 32A-8-6 feeds monitoring findings back into the court file.
relevance.DEC-03: It applies the clear and convincing standard to findings of abuse and neglect that carried forward to termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It is a leading New Mexico Court of Appeals application of the clear and convincing standard to each statutory ground for termination.
relevance.FAIL-06: The court holds that a parent who was warned the Board would report to the court cannot later claim the Board's proceedings were confidential.
relevance.PMC-03: This is the closest New Mexico authority on the legal effect of citizen review board proceedings, which CAPTA Section 5106a(c) requires states to maintain.
relevance.PMC-05: It addresses when assurances of confidentiality in a review process yield to the court's need for the information.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights of Reuben & Elizabeth O.
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that the grounds relied on must be proven by clear and convincing evidence, that evidentiary conflicts are resolved in favor of the prevailing party, and that the department's efforts to assist the parents were reasonable.
cases.quote: The standard of review is whether the grounds relied upon by the district court have been proven by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: It is the foundational New Mexico statement of the burden of proof that a founded finding must satisfy before it can support termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the leading early New Mexico articulation of the clear and convincing standard and the appellate posture for reviewing it.

cases.case_name: In re Termination of Parental Rights of James W.H.
cases.holding: In a matter of first impression the court held that a parent is entitled to effective assistance of counsel in a termination of parental rights proceeding and may raise an ineffectiveness claim on direct appeal, but found no ineffectiveness on this record.
cases.quote: in a termination of parental rights proceeding, a parent is entitled to effective assistance of counsel, and a claim that trial counsel was ineffective may be raised on direct appeal

relevance.OUT-02: It establishes the quality-of-counsel guarantee that attaches to the termination hearing itself.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the New Mexico authority permitting a parent to attack a termination on direct appeal for counsel's ineffectiveness.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Christina L.
cases.holding: The court reversed a neglect adjudication, holding that the district court's findings did not establish that a mental disorder or incapacity was the cause of the mother's inability to care for the child as Section 32A-4-2(E)(4) requires.
cases.quote: We conclude that the district court's findings do not support a determination that Child was neglected pursuant to NMSA 1978, § 32A-4-2(E)(4) (2009)

relevance.INP-10: It shows what an investigation must actually produce before a mental-health-based referral can be escalated to an adjudicated neglect finding.
relevance.DEC-01: It marks the line below which a report should not be founded, because the listed condition must be shown to cause the parenting failure.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling New Mexico case on the proof required for a substantiated finding grounded in a parent's mental disorder or incapacity.
relevance.OUT-05: The adjudication was reversed outright, the appellate route to dismissal when the evidence does not meet the statute.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a clean example of an appellate court vacating an agency-driven finding for insufficient proof.
relevance.FAIL-05: It bars treating a parent's disability as neglect without proof of a causal link, the core anti-disability-discrimination protection in New Mexico adjudications.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Yodell B.
cases.holding: The court held that ICWA's active efforts requirement under 25 U.S.C. Section 1912(d) must be proven by clear and convincing evidence and that the evidence at trial was insufficient, and it reversed the termination of the father's parental rights.
cases.quote: the proper standard of proof for determinations under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) is the clear and convincing standard, which is applicable to the underlying termination of parental rights proceedings

relevance.INP-11: It fixes both the content and the burden of proof of ICWA's active efforts requirement in New Mexico once tribal jurisdiction is triggered.
relevance.FAIL-01: It reversed a termination because the agency's efforts were passive rather than active, a recurring ground of reversal in ICWA cases.
relevance.FAIL-05: Active efforts exist precisely to prevent the breakup of Indian families, and the court's insistence on proof is the enforcement mechanism.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of Ashleigh R.
cases.holding: The court held that the trial court had no authority to appoint guardians over a parent's objection absent proof of present unfitness or extraordinary circumstances, and that voluntary relinquishment of custody plus the children's attachment to the grandparents did not supply those circumstances.
cases.quote: We hold that Grandparents presented insufficient evidence to prove that Mother was unfit to care for her children at the time of the hearing

relevance.INP-05: It arose from a parent's own voluntary handover of her children to relatives without any agency petition.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows the legal consequences of a wholly non-court, family-arranged alternative response and the parental preference that survives it.
relevance.ACT-01: It protects the parent who accepts informal help by refusing to convert voluntary relinquishment into a ground for permanent loss of custody.
relevance.ACT-04: It sets the burden a relative caregiver must meet before a court may formalize a placement over the parent's objection.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the controlling New Mexico statement of the parental preference doctrine that limits guardianship as a permanency outcome.

cases.case_name: Quevedo ex rel. Bevan v. New Mexico Children, Youth & Families Department
cases.holding: The court held that disputed material facts about whether and how CYFD placed children at a private residential ranch precluded summary judgment on whether the Tort Claims Act building waiver in Section 41-4-6(A) permitted suit, and it reversed and remanded.
cases.quote: We conclude that questions of material fact preclude summary judgment on the issue of whether the TCA's building waiver applies to permit Plaintiffs' suit

relevance.ACT-03: It concerns CYFD's responsibility for children it places in a privately operated congregate facility.
relevance.ACT-06: The facility held itself out as providing counseling and therapy to troubled adolescents, so the case bears on state responsibility for court-arranged treatment settings.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the New Mexico vehicle for suing CYFD when children suffer serious harm in a placement the agency arranged.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the narrow Tort Claims Act opening through which harm to children under agency supervision can be litigated in New Mexico.
relevance.PMC-02: The court points to the general appropriations bill and CYFD's funding of the facility as evidence of the agency's operational role.
relevance.PMC-04: Litigation like this is the practical substitute in New Mexico for a published fatality or serious-injury review of a licensed facility.

cases.case_name: Young v. Van Duyne
cases.holding: The court held that sovereign immunity did not bar, at the pleading stage, the claim that CYFD failed before adoption to disclose the child's known dangerous tendencies, but affirmed dismissal of the claims based on CYFD's post-adoption knowledge and conduct.
cases.quote: we remand for further proceedings as to whether Plaintiff can show preadoption circumstances resulting in a breach of a duty to disclose the dangerous tendencies

relevance.OUT-06: The adopted child killed his adoptive mother, and the case sets out when the State may be answerable for that outcome.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the leading New Mexico decision on agency liability for a fatality traceable to withheld placement information.
relevance.PMC-04: It shows how non-disclosure of a child's history surfaces only through wrongful-death litigation rather than public review in New Mexico.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Athena H.
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that a mother's good-faith compliance with her treatment plan does not defeat termination where clear and convincing evidence shows she cannot safely parent within the foreseeable future, and that counsel was not ineffective.
cases.quote: CYFD must provide reasonable efforts to assist the parent to change the conditions that gave rise to the neglect and abuse

relevance.DEC-06: It describes the treatment plan as the framework for CYFD's efforts, which is what an alternative-response service agreement must replicate.
relevance.ACT-01: It confirms that the parent's participation in services is measured against results, not effort alone.
relevance.ACT-02: It is a leading New Mexico statement of the court-approved treatment plan's role and of CYFD's obligation to assist with it.
relevance.OUT-01: It marks the point at which reunification is no longer available despite a compliant parent.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Maria C.
cases.holding: The court held that parents have a due process right to fair notice and meaningful participation at permanency hearings and that the district court must protect a parent's due process rights from the start of the case, but found no due process violation warranting reversal on these facts.
cases.quote: The district court has an affirmative duty to ensure the parents due process rights are protected from the initiation of abuse and neglect proceedings, not just at the end

relevance.OUT-01: It governs the permanency hearing at which the plan may be changed away from reunification and what process the parent is owed there.
relevance.PMC-03: It places the monitoring duty on the district court itself, the oversight body that actually reviews each case in New Mexico.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption Petition of Romero
cases.holding: The court held that a biological father who filed a paternity petition while the adoption was pending was an acknowledged father whose consent was required, and that his pre-birth conduct could not support a finding of presumptive abandonment; it reversed the adoption decree.
cases.quote: Mark's filing of a paternity petition while the adoption proceeding was pending established his status as an acknowledged father according to the plain language of the Act's relevant provisions

relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling New Mexico authority on whose consent an adoption requires and what presumptive abandonment demands.
relevance.OUT-03: It defines the point at which a private placement can be converted into permanent legal status over a parent's objection.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Casey J.
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination and held that CYFD's placement of the children complied with the Abuse and Neglect Act and ICWA because the record supported the district court's finding of good cause to deviate from the ICWA placement preferences, and that the father received due process.
cases.quote: we conclude that the district court did not err in determining that good cause existed to deviate from the ICWA placement preferences at the time of the initial judicial review

relevance.INP-11: It applies ICWA's placement preferences, the federal rule that governs where an Indian child may be placed once tribal jurisdiction is triggered.
relevance.ACT-04: It is New Mexico's leading decision on a parent's ability to force placement with a particular relative and on good cause to deviate from the preferences.
relevance.FAIL-05: Good cause to deviate is the doctrine through which tribal placement preferences are most often defeated, so its contours are where disparate placement outcomes originate.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Arthur C.
cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding the district court did not err in refusing to dismiss the abuse and neglect petition under the amended children's court time-limit rule, and that sufficient evidence supported both the abuse and neglect findings and the finding of active efforts by CYFD.
cases.quote: we hold that there was sufficient evidence to meet the standard of proof for both a finding of abuse and neglect, and a finding of active efforts by CYFD

relevance.INP-04: It construes the children's court rules that govern the timing of adjudicatory hearings once a petition is on file.
relevance.INP-10: It shows the proof an escalated investigation must generate to sustain an adjudication of abuse and neglect.
relevance.DEC-03: It applies the clear and convincing standard to a contested substantiated finding.
relevance.DEC-05: It is the New Mexico authority on when a late adjudicatory hearing does or does not require dismissal of the petition.
relevance.OUT-05: It sets out the district court's discretion to decline dismissal for failure to meet the rule's deadline.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Lance K.
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of the father's parental rights, holding that CYFD relied on stale evidence of conduct years before the hearing so substantial evidence did not support the statutory grounds, while affirming the orders on paternity testing and visitation.
cases.quote: we conclude that substantial evidence does not support termination of Father's parental rights and reverse the judgment on that basis

relevance.OUT-01: It requires that the conditions justifying continued state custody be current, which is what keeps reunification on the table.
relevance.OUT-05: It is a leading New Mexico example of an appellate court unwinding a termination and returning the custody question to the district court.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the clearest New Mexico statement that stale agency evidence cannot sustain a termination.

cases.case_name: Eckhardt v. Charter Hospital of Albuquerque, Inc.
cases.holding: The court held that a counseling center director owed the plaintiff a duty to maintain confidentiality and that good faith alone does not defeat a wrongful-disclosure claim, while identifying the child-abuse reporting statute and its immunity provision as a recognized exception to that duty.
cases.quote: Health-care providers must report actual or suspected cases of child neglect or abuse

relevance.INP-01: It states the health-care provider's reporting obligation and cites Section 32A-4-5(B)'s immunity for reports not made in bad faith or with malicious purpose.
relevance.INP-02: It identifies Section 32A-4-5(B) good-faith immunity as the affirmative defense that protects any person who reports suspected abuse.
relevance.INP-07: It is the New Mexico decision that reconciles a clinician's confidentiality duty with the mandatory child-abuse reporting exception.
relevance.FAIL-06: It sets out when a duty of confidentiality yields to a legal disclosure obligation and when it does not.
relevance.PMC-05: It shows that good faith alone does not justify releasing protected information absent a statutory reporting exception.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Anne McD.
cases.holding: Applying the Mathews balancing test, the court held that allowing six of CYFD's seven witnesses to testify by telephone did not deny the mother procedural due process and that clear and convincing evidence supported the termination.
cases.quote: we conclude that the Children's Court did not deny procedural due process to Mother

relevance.DEC-05: It is the New Mexico case importing the Mathews framework into children's court practice from the filing of the petition forward.
relevance.OUT-01: It reviews the reasonable-efforts finding that had to fail before reunification could be abandoned.

cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children Youth and Family Department
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for the CYFD social worker and county officers who entered a New Mexico home without a warrant and removed two children, and clarified that warrantless entry or seizure in the child welfare context requires a threat of imminent harm under both the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments.
cases.quote: even in the child welfare context, there must be a threat of imminent harm when officials enter a home or seize children without a warrant or judicial authorization

relevance.INP-01: The case was triggered by the child's teacher, a mandatory reporter, whose classroom observations and the child's disclosure generated the report.
relevance.INP-02: It traces what happens after a report is made by a person with no statutory duty to make it in the way she did.
relevance.INP-03: CYFD and several law-enforcement officers acted jointly within hours of the report, the coordinated response this node describes.
relevance.INP-06: The report was made anonymously to the CYFD hotline, and the opinion examines what that intake report did and did not establish.
relevance.INP-08: The disclosure originated in a classroom and the teacher's observations of the child's behavior at school.
relevance.INP-10: It shows the speed and thinness of the escalation from a single intake report to a warrantless home entry.
relevance.INP-12: This is the controlling Tenth Circuit statement of the exigency required before protective custody may be taken without judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-02: The Court rejects any social-worker exception to the Fourth Amendment for investigative entries into a home.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the governing circuit authority, decided on New Mexico facts, for whether an emergency removal was constitutionally justified.
relevance.ACT-05: The second removal followed the father's anticipated release from jail, showing how a no-contact objective is pursued through removal rather than a protective order.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the single most important recent decision on Section 1983 liability for allegedly unlawful removal by New Mexico child-welfare officials.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the current outer boundary of federal accountability for New Mexico removal practice and the baseline for any systemic critique.

cases.case_name: Doe v. Woodard
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal on qualified immunity, holding the plaintiffs did not show clearly established law that the special needs doctrine could not justify a caseworker's warrantless visual body search of a four-year-old at school, and that the Fourteenth Amendment claims failed to state a claim.
cases.quote: We conclude they have not shown clearly established law that the special needs doctrine could not support the search in this case

relevance.INP-06: The search followed an anonymous abuse report, and the opinion addresses how far such a report lets a caseworker go.
relevance.INP-07: A caseworker's visual inspection of a child's body is an examination for physical indicators of abuse, and this case sets its constitutional frame.
relevance.INP-08: The search took place at the child's school without parental notice or consent.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the governing circuit authority on whether a caseworker may search a child's body during an investigation without a warrant or parental consent.
relevance.ACT-06: It addresses the legal status of a quasi-medical examination performed on a child by agency staff rather than a clinician.
relevance.FAIL-02: It shows how qualified immunity defeats damages claims for investigative intrusions even where the constitutional question remains open.

cases.case_name: Malik v. Arapahoe County Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity to caseworkers, holding it was clearly established that a parent's liberty interest in familial association cannot be taken without adequate pre-deprivation procedures absent extraordinary circumstances, and that an ex parte order procured by misrepresentation and omission is no substitute.
cases.quote: An ex parte hearing based on misrepresentation and omission does not constitute notice and an opportunity to be heard

relevance.INP-03: The removal was planned jointly by the department and the city police department, the coordinated posture this node describes.
relevance.INP-12: It marks the constitutional limit on taking a child into protective custody without a genuine emergency.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the leading Tenth Circuit decision on the process owed before an emergency removal and on ex parte orders obtained by incomplete affidavits.
relevance.ACT-05: It addresses the state's use of an ex parte court order as the instrument for separating a child from a parent.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the circuit's core authority for Section 1983 liability where the removal order rests on caseworker misrepresentation.

cases.case_name: Yvonne L. v. New Mexico Department of Human Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that children in New Mexico state custody had a clearly established Fourteenth Amendment right to reasonable safety measured by the Youngberg professional judgment standard and reversed qualified immunity on that claim, while affirming that 42 U.S.C. Section 671(a)(10) of the AACWA is too vague and amorphous to be enforced under Section 1983.
cases.quote: while it does not require actual knowledge the children will be harmed, it implies abdication of the duty to act professionally in making the placements

relevance.INP-09: The plaintiffs' theory was that New Mexico never designated an authority or adopted standards for child care institutions, an oversight failure the court examines.
relevance.DEC-01: The court's professional-judgment standard reaches decisions not to screen or separate dangerous residents, the institutional analogue of a bad screening decision.
relevance.ACT-03: It is the controlling circuit authority, arising from New Mexico, on the State's duty once it places a child in substitute care.
relevance.OUT-06: It supplies the liability standard when children in New Mexico state custody are seriously harmed in placement.
relevance.FAIL-03: It holds that the AACWA's national-standards provision is not privately enforceable, so federal compliance failures are policed by the funding agency rather than by damages suits.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the professional-judgment abdication that converts a placement decision into a constitutional violation.
relevance.PMC-01: It shows why CFSR and federal plan review, not private litigation, are the operative checks on state-plan compliance.
relevance.PMC-02: Because Section 671(a)(10) is not judicially enforceable, audit and funding mechanisms carry the burden of enforcing institutional standards.

cases.case_name: Jones v. Hunt
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a New Mexico CYFD social work supervisor who, together with a deputy sheriff, confronted a student at her high school until she agreed to live with her father violated her clearly established Fourth Amendment right to be free of unreasonable seizure, and reversed the dismissal of her Section 1983 suit.
cases.quote: we conclude that she has alleged sufficient facts to demonstrate at the 12(B)(6) stage that she was unreasonably seized within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment

relevance.INP-03: The seizure was carried out jointly by a sheriff's deputy and a CYFD supervisor, the paradigm of a coordinated law-enforcement and CPS contact.
relevance.INP-08: The entire encounter occurred in a school office during the school day, without the mother's knowledge.
relevance.INP-12: It marks the constitutional limit on coercive custody decisions made outside any court process.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the governing circuit authority on when a child-welfare interview of a child becomes an unreasonable seizure.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that a de facto custody change engineered by state officials without judicial authorization is a seizure that must be reasonable.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading New Mexico-based Tenth Circuit case allowing a Section 1983 claim against a CYFD official for an unlawful child seizure.

cases.case_name: Schwartz v. Booker
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who failed to investigate abuse referrals and closed a foster child's case before he was starved and beaten to death were not entitled to qualified immunity, because the special relationship with a child in state custody and his right to reasonable safety were clearly established.
cases.quote: plaintiffs sufficiently pled facts, when taken as true, that show Booker and Peagler plausibly violated Chandler's substantive due process right to be reasonably safe while in foster care

relevance.INP-10: It holds that the duty to investigate persists for a child already in custody, so new referrals must be escalated rather than closed.
relevance.DEC-01: Dismissing a foster child's case without investigating the referrals is precisely the screen-out failure this node covers, and here it defeated qualified immunity.
relevance.ACT-03: It confirms that the state's custodial duty continues for the whole duration of the placement, not just at the moment of placement.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the circuit's leading decision on caseworker liability for a child's death in foster care.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the controlling authority for holding individual caseworkers answerable for a fatality under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: The facts illustrate exactly what a fatality review is supposed to surface: unexamined referrals and a case closed without investigation.

cases.case_name: T.D. v. Patton
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a caseworker who recommended and maintained a child's placement with a father she had reason to believe was abusing him, and who withheld her concerns from the juvenile court, violated the child's clearly established substantive due process right to be free from state-created danger.
cases.quote: we conclude that, under Currier, Ms. Patton violated T.D.'s clearly established substantive due process constitutional right to be free of a state official's creation of danger from a private actor

relevance.ACT-03: It defines the caseworker's affirmative duties when recommending and continuing a placement for a child in state custody.
relevance.OUT-06: It supplies the standard for caseworker liability when a placement decision leads to severe abuse of a child in care.
relevance.FAIL-02: It holds that misleading or incomplete statements to the court that shape a placement decision expose the caseworker to Section 1983 liability.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the circuit's clearest statement that failure to investigate evidence of abuse in an existing placement is itself actionable.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may sever the rights of parents in their natural child, the Due Process Clause requires the State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process

relevance.DEC-03: It is the federal constitutional floor that New Mexico's clear and convincing standard for founded findings and termination implements.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling federal constitutional standard of proof for every termination of parental rights.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. Section 671(a)(15), confers no enforceable private right on its beneficiaries and creates no implied cause of action.
cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf

relevance.INP-09: It explains why federal child-welfare performance requirements are enforced through the Secretary's plan-approval and review machinery rather than private suits.
relevance.OUT-04: Extended foster care and transition supports rest on the same Title IV-E state-plan structure, which this case holds is not privately enforceable.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the controlling authority on the remedy, or absence of one, for a state's failure to meet federal child-welfare plan requirements.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR review exists because Suter leaves federal plan compliance to the funding agency rather than to litigants.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial audit and corrective action are the operative enforcement tools precisely because Suter forecloses private enforcement.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis of New Mexico's federal compliance must begin from the premise that private enforcement of IV-E requirements is unavailable.

cases.case_name: Roth v. Bookert
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the judgment voiding the proposed adoption but overruled the Court of Appeals' treatment of the presumptive-abandonment statute, holding that no separate finding of parental unfitness is required to terminate under that statute, that the presumption of abandonment is rebutted by showing the parent lacks responsibility for the disintegration of the parent-child relationship, and that on this record the presumption was rebutted as a matter of law; it remanded the custody question.
cases.quote: the presumption of abandonment established by the conditions set forth in Section 32-1-54(B)(4) may be rebutted by showing that a parent lacks responsibility for the disintegration of the parent-child relationship

relevance.OUT-02: It is the New Mexico Supreme Court's foundational construction of presumptive abandonment as a ground for severing a parent's rights in a contested adoption, and it holds that the presumption collapses once the parent shows he did not cause the relationship's breakdown.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Ruth Anne E.
cases.holding: Applying the Mathews balancing test, the court held that an incarcerated parent who cannot attend the termination hearing is entitled to meaningful participation rather than merely cross-examination, argument through counsel, or deposition testimony, and it reversed the termination and remanded for a new hearing.
cases.quote: he or she has the right to meaningful participation in the hearing

relevance.DEC-05: It fixes the procedural floor the children's court owes a parent once the State's petition is on file, holding that a hearing the parent cannot meaningfully join does not satisfy due process.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Steven
cases.holding: The court held that where the mother had been involuntarily deported to Mexico and the termination hearing proceeded in her absence, the trial court had an affirmative responsibility to inquire whether she had waived her due process rights, and it reversed and remanded for further proceedings.
cases.quote: we hold that the trial court had a responsibility to inquire into whether Mother had waived her due process rights

relevance.DEC-05: Once the petition is filed the children's court itself bears the duty to establish on the record that an absent parent validly waived participation, which is the safeguard that makes the proceeding lawful.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Vanessa C.
cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination, holding that the standard of proof is clear and convincing evidence, that the district court did not err in basing a futility finding made at a judicial review hearing on unobjected-to hearsay, and that the procedures used did not violate the mother's due process rights.
cases.quote: The standard of proof in cases involving the termination of parental rights is clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-05: It is the standard New Mexico statement of the burden of proof and of the Mathews due-process balancing that governs the judicial review and futility findings made after a dependency case is opened.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Patricia H.
cases.holding: The court affirmed the termination, holding that CYFD's statutory obligation to make reasonable efforts to assist the parent is a prerequisite to termination, that what is reasonable varies with the parent's cooperation and the recalcitrance of the problems, and that the appellate task is limited to asking whether CYFD complied with the minimum required by law, which it did here.
cases.quote: The statutory prerequisite of reasonable efforts to assist the parent must be satisfied before parental rights may be terminated

relevance.ACT-02: It is the New Mexico source of the reasonable-efforts formulation courts apply to a court-approved treatment plan, and it holds the assistance obligation is a condition precedent rather than an afterthought.
relevance.OUT-01: It measures how long and how intensively CYFD must work toward reunification, drawing on ASFA's fifteen-month time-limited reunification period, before the plan may be abandoned.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Shawna C.
cases.holding: The court affirmed the abuse and neglect adjudication as to the mother, reversed it as to the father for insufficient evidence, and held that the Abuse and Neglect Act's definitions are not so vague as to violate substantive due process.
cases.quote: we hold that the abuse and neglect statute is not so vague as to violate substantive due process protections under the United States Constitution

relevance.DEC-03: It applies the clear and convincing standard separately to each parent and rejects the vagueness attack on the statutory definitions that every substantiated finding in New Mexico rests upon.
relevance.FAIL-01: The adjudication against the father was reversed outright for want of clear and convincing evidence, a direct instance of a court undoing an agency-driven finding.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Amanda H.
cases.holding: The court reversed a neglect adjudication because inconclusive toxicology evidence could not meet the clear and convincing standard, and held that a sufficiency challenge to an abuse or neglect adjudication is not rendered moot by the district court's dismissal of the underlying case while the appeal is pending.
cases.quote: The standard of proof in an abuse or neglect adjudication is clear and convincing evidence that the child was abused or neglected

relevance.DEC-03: It states the burden and the narrow standard of review governing every contested substantiated finding in New Mexico, and requires proof of the parent's intentional or negligent disregard of the child's needs.
relevance.OUT-05: It holds that dismissal of the underlying case does not moot the parent's challenge, so an erroneous adjudication can still be stricken after the case closes.

cases.case_name: M.D.R. v. State ex rel. Human Services Department
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal on sovereign immunity grounds, holding that the Tort Claims Act does not waive the State's immunity for the department's foster placement and supervision of children because placing a child in a foster home is neither the provision of 'health care services' under Section 41-4-10 nor the operation of a hospital or 'like facility' under Section 41-4-9.
cases.quote: While the complaint alleges deplorable conduct by the Department, the Act does not waive the State's immunity from tort liability under the circumstances of this case

relevance.ACT-03: It is the governing New Mexico decision on how far the State may be held answerable in tort for the foster placements it makes and supervises.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the immunity backdrop against which Quevedo and Young v. Van Duyne must be read, and it explains why most harm to children under New Mexico agency supervision never reaches a jury.

cases.case_name: San Juan Agricultural Water Users Ass'n v. KNME-TV
cases.holding: The Court held that a principal, disclosed or not, may delegate the making of an Inspection of Public Records Act request to an agent such as counsel, and that either the agent or the principal may sue to enforce the request if it is denied; it reversed the dismissal of the association's claims.
cases.quote: a principal, whether disclosed or not, can delegate the function of requesting public records to an agent, such as the principal's attorney

relevance.FAIL-06: It removes the standing objection agencies raise when a records request was submitted through counsel or an intermediary, which is how most child-welfare records requests are actually made.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the New Mexico Supreme Court's controlling statement of who may make and who may enforce an IPRA request, the state analogue to a FOIA requester's right of action.

cases.case_name: Currier v. Doran
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that DeShaney does not foreclose a substantive due process claim where state officials affirmatively created or increased the danger to a child, affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to two New Mexico child-welfare defendants whose conduct placed the children with the father who killed one of them, and reversed the denial of immunity as to two other defendants.
cases.quote: The danger creation theory, however, focuses on the affirmative actions of the state in placing the plaintiff in harm's way

relevance.OUT-06: A child died of his father's abuse after state officials' conduct moved him into that home, and this opinion supplies the circuit standard for holding the State answerable for that death.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the New Mexico-arising Tenth Circuit precedent establishing danger-creation liability under Section 1983 for child-welfare officials, and it is the authority T.D. v. Patton applies.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the affirmative-conduct element that converts a caseworker's custody recommendation into a constitutional violation when the child is then killed or seriously injured.

cases.case_name: Gomes v. Wood
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court adopted the reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removals, holding that officials may remove a child without prior notice and a hearing when they reasonably suspect an immediate threat to the child's safety, that the parents must still receive a prompt post-removal hearing, and that the defendants here did not violate clearly established law and were entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: officials may remove a child from the home without prior notice and a hearing when they have a reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the safety of the child

relevance.DEC-04: It supplies the reasonable-suspicion-of-immediate-threat test that governs every warrantless emergency removal in the Tenth Circuit, and it is the framework Lowther later clarifies rather than overrules.
relevance.INP-12: It holds that even a justified emergency taking of protective custody must be followed by a prompt post-removal hearing, and that the availability of judicial authorization is one relevant circumstance.

cases.case_name: Dubbs ex rel. Dubbs v. Head Start, Inc.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that physical and blood examinations of Head Start children conducted without parental consent were searches for Fourth Amendment purposes, that the record permitted a finding they were not consensual, and that the special needs doctrine would not excuse the failure to obtain parental consent; it reversed summary judgment on the Fourth Amendment and related claims.
cases.quote: we conclude that the "special needs doctrine" would not excuse the failure to obtain parental consent for the examinations

relevance.DEC-02: It is the circuit's leading holding that a non-consensual physical examination of a child by program staff is a Fourth Amendment search requiring more justification than administrative convenience.
relevance.INP-07: It governs the constitutional status of a physical and blood examination performed on a child to detect health or abuse indicators without the parents' knowledge or consent.
relevance.INP-08: The examinations were carried out at the children's preschool program without notice to the parents, the same school-setting intrusion Doe v. Woodard later addressed.

cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that Spending Clause legislation can create rights enforceable under Section 1983 where the statute unambiguously confers individual federal rights, that the two Federal Nursing Home Reform Act provisions at issue did so, and that nothing in the Act's enforcement scheme impliedly precluded Section 1983 suits; it affirmed.
cases.quote: In that respect, our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights

relevance.FAIL-03: It supplies the current Supreme Court test for whether any federal child-welfare plan requirement is privately enforceable, and it must be applied before Suter's reasoning is relied on.
relevance.PMC-01: It restates that the typical remedy for a State's non-compliance with a Spending Clause statute is termination of funds, which is exactly the CFSR and program-improvement machinery.
relevance.PMC-02: Because the ordinary consequence of non-compliance is defunding rather than damages, audit and corrective-action processes remain the operative enforcement tools, and this is the Court's current statement of that rule.

cases.case_name: Nguyen v. Bui
cases.holding: The Court held that the plain language of the Family Violence Protection Act does not require a petitioner to show imminent danger or injury to obtain an order of protection, and it affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the denial of an order to a petitioner who alleged she was sexually assaulted as a child.
cases.quote: We hold that the plain language of the FVPA does not require petitioners to provide a showing of imminent danger or injury in seeking an order of protection

relevance.ACT-05: It is the New Mexico Supreme Court's controlling construction of the Family Violence Protection Act, the statute under which a protective order is obtained to keep an abuser away without removing the child, and it removes the imminence barrier that had been imposed on child sexual-abuse petitioners.

CourtListener's court metadata is wrong for two clusters: State v. Strauch (cluster 6592364) and State ex rel. CYFD v. Djamila B. (cluster 6592326) are labelled court_id 'nmctapp' in the API, but both are New Mexico SUPREME COURT opinions (2015-NMSC-009 and 2015-NMSC-003 respectively, per the opinion text and the cluster's own vendor-neutral citation). This brief reports the correct court; expect a mismatch if the entry is machine-checked against the CourtListener court field.

Four opinions are stored by CourtListener as text that embeds the New Mexico Compilation Commission's marginal LINE NUMBERS inside the running text (e.g. 'reasonable efforts to fix 12 the problem'). The quotes for Yodell B. (cluster 3165056), Casey J. (cluster 2811407), Pacheco v. Hudson (cluster 4474535) and Calvin T. (cluster 10699659) are exact substrings of those opinions ONLY after the marginal numerals are stripped; they are verbatim as published. The Keon H. quote was deliberately chosen to fall entirely within a single line so that it matches the stored text as-is.

Vendor-neutral citations: New Mexico's official citation form is the public-domain '20XX-NMSC-0NN' / '20XX-NMCA-0NN' number. Where the CourtListener cluster carried no citation at all, slip form is used as instructed; note that State ex rel. CYFD v. Douglas B. (cluster 10701733) is officially 2023-NMSC-028 and State ex rel. CYFD v. Calvin T. (cluster 10699659) is a July 3, 2025 slip opinion not yet assigned a vendor-neutral number in CourtListener. The '7 N.M. 422' and '9 N.M. 503' style citations that appear in CourtListener's NM clusters are an artifact of a bulk import and are NOT usable Bluebook citations; they were ignored.

OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out) has no published New Mexico appellate authority. Targeted searches of both nm and nmctapp for extended foster care, transition plans, jurisdiction past age eighteen and Chafee/FCSIAA supports returned nothing on point. The node is populated with the two New Mexico Supreme Court decisions that actually involve older youth in long-term CYFD custody (Calvin T., where the youth had been in custody since 2015 and faced discharge from acute care with no placement identified, and Mercer-Smith, where the Court records that the children aged out during the litigation) plus Suter v. Artist M. for the federal Title IV-E state-plan framework on which extended care rests. A practitioner should treat NMSA 1978, Section 32A-4-25.3 and CYFD's Fostering Connections rules as the operative law here, not case law.

FAIL-03 (Federal Compliance Failure), PMC-01 (CFSR) and PMC-02 (OIG/Single Audit) likewise have no New Mexico case law. They are given the federal standard: Suter v. Artist M. (no private enforcement of the Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' plan requirement) and Yvonne L. v. New Mexico DHS (Section 671(a)(10)'s national-standards clause too vague and amorphous to be enforced under Section 1983). Note that Suter was partially superseded for other IV-E provisions by 42 U.S.C. Section 1320a-2 (the 'Suter fix'), which provides that a provision is not to be deemed unenforceable solely because it is contained in a state plan; Section 1320a-2 expressly does not disturb Suter's actual holding on Section 671(a)(15). Health & Hospital Corp. v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023), is the current Supreme Court framework for spending-clause Section 1983 claims and should be consulted before relying on Suter's reasoning.

PMC-03 (Citizen Review Panels): New Mexico's substitute care review boards are governed by NMSA 1978, Section 32A-8-6. In re Termination of Parental Rights of Eventyr J. is the only published New Mexico decision located that analyses the legal effect of those board proceedings, and it holds that a parent who was told the board would report to the court cannot later claim the board proceedings were confidential. There is no published New Mexico authority on the independence or public reporting of CAPTA Section 5106a(c) citizen review panels.

PMC-04 (Fatality Review Commission) and OUT-06/FAIL-04 have no published New Mexico decision reviewing a child-fatality review report. The nodes are populated with the actual liability vehicles in this jurisdiction: Quevedo (New Mexico Tort Claims Act building waiver as the route to suing CYFD), Young v. Van Duyne (pre-adoption failure to disclose dangerous propensities, where the adopted child killed his adoptive mother), and the Tenth Circuit's Schwartz v. Booker and T.D. v. Patton. Lawyers should note that M.D.R. v. State ex rel. Human Services Department, 114 N.M. 187, 836 P.2d 106 (Ct. App. 1992), read together with Young, means CYFD's negligent placement decisions are generally immune under the Tort Claims Act unless a specific waiver applies.

FAIL-05 (Discrimination / Retaliation): no published New Mexico child-welfare decision applies the New Mexico Human Rights Act, Title VI, or the ADA to a CPS investigation or placement. The node is built from the two anti-disparity doctrines that New Mexico courts do enforce: ICWA (Yodell B., Casey J., Douglas B., In re Esther V.) and the Christina L. rule that a parent's mental disorder cannot found a neglect adjudication without proof it caused the parenting failure. Malik v. Arapahoe County is the Tenth Circuit's retaliation case (caseworker retaliation against a mother for retaining counsel) and is a useful analogue although it arises from Colorado.

ACT-06 (Emergency Medical/Psychological Care): searches for court-ordered or emergency medical treatment of a child in state custody returned no squarely on-point published New Mexico decision. Calvin T. (2025) is the closest authority, arising from a youth in CYFD custody facing discharge from acute psychiatric care with no treatment foster placement available; it establishes the joinder mechanism by which a child can bring a managed care organization into the abuse and neglect case. Practitioners should also consult NMSA 1978, Sections 32A-6A-1 to -30 (Children's Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities Act).

Several New Mexico cases exist in CourtListener as duplicate clusters (for example Marlene C. appears as clusters 891709 and 2358810; Djamila B. as 6592326, 2672329 and 2653487). The cluster chosen in each entry is the one carrying reporter or vendor-neutral citations and full opinion text. State ex rel. CYFD v. Marlene C., 2009-NMCA-058 (cluster 2590301) was read but is not included because the Supreme Court granted certiorari and decided the same case as In re Esther V., 2011-NMSC-005, which supersedes it. The Court of Appeals opinion in Keon H., 2017-NMCA-004, and the Court of Appeals opinion in Mercer-Smith, 2015-NMCA-093, were both read and both excluded because the New Mexico Supreme Court reversed them.

Caution on Kennedy v. Dexter Consolidated Schools: the entry is the 2000 NEW MEXICO SUPREME COURT decision (cluster 2632200), which reversed in part the Court of Appeals decision at 1998-NMCA-051 (cluster 1242299). Cite only the Supreme Court opinion. It is a school-search case rather than a CPS case; it is mapped only to INP-08 and DEC-02, where it supplies New Mexico's individualized-suspicion rule for intrusive searches of a child at school.

New Mexico sits in the Tenth Circuit, so Lowther v. CYFD (2024, arising from New Mexico), Jones v. Hunt (2005, arising from New Mexico) and Yvonne L. v. New Mexico DHS (1992, arising from New Mexico) are binding federal authority on New Mexico removals and foster-care liability. Lowther is the most recent and most important: it resolves an ambiguity in Gomes v. Wood and holds that a threat of IMMINENT harm is required under both the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments before a warrantless entry or seizure of a child.

Statutory context relied on when framing relevance, taken from the NM node files and the opinions read: NMSA 1978, Section 32A-4-3(A) and (F) (universal duty to report; failure to report is a misdemeanor), Section 32A-4-5(B) (reporter immunity absent bad faith or malicious purpose), Section 32A-4-18 (custody hearings), Sections 32A-4-20(G)-(H) (adjudicatory hearing; clear and convincing evidence), Section 32A-4-22(C) (reasonable efforts, child's health and safety paramount), Section 32A-4-28(B) (grounds for termination), Section 32A-4-29(I)-(L) (TPR procedure and burden), Sections 40-10B-1 to -15 (Kinship Guardianship Act), Section 32A-8-6 (substitute care review boards), and Sections 14-2-1 to -12 (Inspection of Public Records Act).
